column10:
Here’s a plain-language answer for Asim:

When an investment firm or a wealthy family’s office buys a small or mid-size company, they have a few months to check what they’re really buying before they hand over millions of dollars. That checking is called due diligence.

We do the hands-on part of that checking. We look at how the company actually runs: how it makes its products, who its customers are, whether the owner is holding everything together personally, and whether the numbers the seller shows hold up in real life. We also keep the buyer’s accountants and lawyers working to one plan and one timeline.

When we find a problem, we help the buyer turn it into a better price or safer deal terms, so they don’t overpay.

Before the deal closes, we hand them a plain operating playbook: the first things to fix, the risks to watch, and the opportunities to capture in their first year of owning the company.

We charge a monthly fee for the months the deal is being checked and closed.

In one line, if he needs it: “We help investors check a company before they buy it, so they pay the right price and know what to do on day one.”

column12:
We don’t guarantee deal outcomes; no honest advisor can. We do reduce the risk of hiring us. Buyers can start with a short fixed-price red-flag review, credited in full if they continue. After a one-month minimum, the engagement is month to month and can be cancelled with 15 days’ notice. We commit to a first red-flag summary within 10 business days of data room access. Early clients also get a reduced rate in exchange for a case study.
Example:

A buyer pays $5,000 for the red-flag review.
You find a customer who makes up 40% of revenue and an inventory problem.
They hire you for the full engagement at $12,000 a month.
Their first month’s bill is $12,000 minus $5,000, so $7,000.

Why it works: the buyer tests me with little risk, I get paid for my time either way, and most buyers who see real findings continue.
column13:
“Senior, hands-on operational diligence from a former founder and CEO who has also sold founder-owned companies, at a price that works for lower middle market deals.”

1. Boutique diligence and advisory firms

Who they are: full teams charging around $40,000 a month, mostly on deals of $50M and up.
How we’re different: a senior advisor does the work directly, at a fraction of the cost. We’re built for the smaller deals they don’t prioritize.

2. Accounting firms doing quality of earnings reports

Who they are: they check whether the financial numbers are accurate.
How we’re different: we check the operations behind the numbers: how the business really runs, whether it depends on the owner, customer and supplier risk, and whether costing and inventory hold up. We bring the financial analysis that ties operations to the numbers, such as margins, costing and working capital, and we coordinate with the accountants and lawyers rather than replacing them.

3. Independent operating consultants and fractional executives

Who they are: experienced operators, often brought in after closing.
How we’re different: we come from the deal side. We’ve sold founder-owned companies, so we know where the risks hide and how to turn findings into price and terms before closing, not after.

What only we bring:

A founder’s view. We’ve built and exited a company ourselves, and also sold founder-owned businesses for their owners.
Sell-side experience on founder-owned businesses. We’ve seen deals stall on an IP claim, a work-in-progress dispute and owner dependence, and we know what to look for.
One coordinated diligence process across operations, the accountants and the lawyers, with findings in one place.
Findings turned into the deal: price, working capital, escrow and earnout recommendations, not just a report.
An operating playbook for year one, ready at closing.

column23:
A qualified prospect is a decision maker at a private equity firm, independent sponsor or family office who passes four tests:

Capacity: they have capital or committed backers to do deals in our range, roughly $3M to $50M in revenue, and budget for outside help.
Credibility: they’ve done deals before, or are clearly set up to, not just exploring.
Clarity: they know what they’re looking for: a defined investment thesis or a specific target.
Commitment: they’re actively looking for acquisitions in the next 6 to 12 months, or evaluating a specific deal now.

Strongest fit: they don’t have a full in-house diligence team, which applies to most independent sponsors and smaller family offices.

Not qualified: search funds, browsers with no capital, brokers posing as buyers, and established firms with full in-house deal teams.
